- Our primary SLO target is p95 latency <= 200ms for typical user requests. Typical request size is ~512 tokens in, ~256 tokens out.
- Expected peak concurrency: 40 concurrent sessions.
- Sustained throughput target during peak: ~120 requests/sec.
- Streaming is important: we rely on partial output for UX.
- We also need guidance on how context window (8k vs 32k) will change latency and cost per request.

Can you confirm whether those numbers look feasible on Redwood Dedicated or Hosted, and what trade-offs you recommend (batching, quantization, model variant)? If possible please include a short canary plan and any attachments we can pass to procurement.

Hi Sarah — thanks for the clear summary. Below is a short technical recap plus recommended next steps. I've attached a short capacity plan PDF for procurement.

Recap of your targets (as I understood them):
- p95 latency <= 200ms for ~512 in / ~256 out
- concurrency: 40 sessions
- throughput: ~120 req/s at peak
- streaming required (server-sent partial tokens)

High-level feasibility
- Hosted API: possible but depends on burst capacity and reserved throughput; we'd recommend Redwood Dedicated for predictable p95 at that concurrency.
- Dedicated: with the config below we expect to meet the p95 target for a 512/256 profile on a 32-bit quantized LLM variant and with aggressive prefix caching.

Key trade-offs and notes
- Context window: moving from 8k -> 32k increases memory use and KV-cache lookups, which raises per-token latency by ~15-30% in our measurements at moderate sequence lengths (all else equal). The biggest latency driver is attention ops for long inputs — if your traffic has many long-history cases we'll need either a larger instance class or to use smarter prefix caching.
- Batching: batching improves throughput but adds headroom latency. For a 200ms p95 we limit batch waits to ~5-10ms and rely on concurrency to keep GPUs utilized.
- Streaming: streaming has negligible extra server-side overhead for token flushing, but enabling low-latency streaming requires smaller generation step sizes (e.g., flush every 8–16 tokens) which can slightly increase compute overhead and therefore per-token cost.
- Quantization & model variant: int8/4 quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput; however, extreme quant (4-bit) can slightly increase generation time per token and may affect output quality.

Recommended config for a canary (estimate)
- Model variant: rwl-13b-quant-int8 (or rwl-13b-8k if you need cheaper 8k profiles)
- Instance class: 2x A100 equivalent (or Dedicated pool with 8x smaller GPUs depending on concurrency pattern)
- Autoscale: maintain min capacity to support 40 concurrent sessions, scale to handle 2x burst (240 req/s)
- Batching policy: max batch wait 10ms; dynamic batching by latency SLO
- Cache policy: prefix KV cache for authenticated sessions, TTL 30 minutes
- Streaming: enable flush every 12 tokens

Next steps
1) Connor to provide a short breakdown of compute vs latency for 512/256 and 8k/32k windows (see his note below).
2) We share the attached PDF (redwood-slo-capacity-plan.pdf) for procurement.
3) Quick 30-min follow-up call to validate numbers and agree on canary scope.

I'll leave Connor to add the compute numbers. Happy to jump on a call Thursday or Friday morning PT.

Best,

Hi all — quick technical addendum with measured numbers (lab estimates) to help validate the canary sizing. These assume a tuned runtime and an optimized model variant (rwl-13b-quant-int8).

Baseline numbers (single instance behavior, median of multiple runs)
- 512 in / 256 out, 8k context kernel path: per-token compute time ~1.6ms, end-to-end median latency ~120ms, p95 ~190–220ms depending on batch timing.
- 512 in / 256 out, 32k context kernel path: per-token compute time increases to ~1.9–2.0ms (KV lookups + larger attention windows), end-to-end median ~150ms, p95 ~230–260ms.

Concurrency and batching impact (observed)
- With 40 concurrent sessions and batch wait limited to 10ms, effective throughput ~100–140 req/s depending on sequence-length distribution.
- If you permit batch-waits up to 25ms, throughput improves (~160–200 req/s) but p95 shifts higher (by ~30–50ms).

Streaming notes
- Flushing every 12 tokens adds ~3–6% compute overhead vs. single-block completion due to extra I/O events. In practice we still meet 200ms p95 for the 8k path if instance sizing is adequate.

Operational recommendations
- Start canary with a single Dedicated pool sized for 40 concurrent sessions (reserve capacity), run traffic at 10–20% of expected peak for 72 hours to validate p95 and throughput.
- Instrument token-level latency and per-request batch wait time; link metrics back to user sessions for correlation.
- If using 32k windows frequently, increase instance class or enable session-level partial context (trim older context server-side) to keep latency in-check.

I'll prepare a short spreadsheet with these numbers for the call — attaching a lightweight CSV in the drive link Marissa listed.

Thanks,
Connor Obrien
